subject: Coffee & Tea
title: Iced Tea's Accidental Birth
description: A micro-lesson that makes Iced Tea's Accidental Birth usable.

hook.text: At the 1904 St. Louis World's Fair, a tea merchant's hot samples went ignored in the sweltering heat.

buildup.text: Richard Blechynden watched visitors walk past his booth to buy cold drinks. Sales were zero.

discovery.text: In desperation, he poured his hot tea over ice. The crowd rushed in. Iced tea was an instant hit.

twist.text: Iced tea now accounts for about 80% of all tea consumed in the United States.

climax.text: Sweet tea in the American South became a cultural icon—so important some call it 'the table wine of the South.'

punchline.text: A hot day, no customers, and a desperate idea changed everything.

quiz.question: What percentage of tea consumed in the U.S. is iced?

details.summary: Iced tea was popularized at the 1904 St. Louis World's Fair when tea merchant Richard Blechynden could not sell hot tea in the summer heat. He poured it over ice and created a sensation. Iced tea became an American staple and now accounts for over 80 percent of US tea consumption.
details.whyItMatters: Iced tea shows how environmental necessity breeds innovation. A hot day at a world's fair created the dominant way America drinks tea over a century later.
takeaways: Iced tea was popularized at the 1904 St. Louis World's Fair
Richard Blechynden poured hot tea over ice out of desperation
Iced tea now accounts for over 80 percent of US consumption

faq.question: Was iced tea really invented at the 1904 World's Fair?
faq.answer: Not exactly invented, as cold tea recipes existed earlier. But the World's Fair popularized iced tea on a massive scale. Blechynden's success at the fair created widespread awareness and demand. The hot climate of St. Louis made cold tea an obvious hit with fairgoers.

faq.question: Why does the American South drink so much sweet iced tea?
faq.answer: The South's hot climate makes cold drinks essential. Sugar was historically abundant and cheap in the region. Sweet tea became a symbol of Southern hospitality and identity. It is served with meals, at gatherings, and in restaurants as a default beverage in many Southern states.
